cm6_clarity_of_research_objectives.reason: The paper clearly states both research questions/hypotheses and specific application purposes. Step 1: The abstract explicitly states the objective to 'accommodate for these site effects by including them as random effects in a hierarchical Bayesian model.' Step 2: The introduction clearly articulates the research gap - that site effects are confounded with variables of interest in multi-site neuroimaging. Step 3: The paper specifies the application purpose - to enable normative modeling on large multi-site datasets while retaining clinically useful information. Step 4: Three specific aims are described: (1) comparing hierarchical Bayesian models to harmonization techniques, (2) evaluating whether models remove site effects, and (3) testing whether models retain clinically relevant variance. Both assessment criteria are met at >80%.

common_part.cm7_additional_comments: This is a methodological paper focused on developing and validating hierarchical Bayesian approaches for normative modeling in multi-site neuroimaging data. The paper extends prior work by Kia et al. (2020) by adding Gaussian Process regression for non-linear modeling. The study uses the publicly available ABIDE dataset. Code is made publicly available on GitHub. The paper includes extensive supplementary materials with model diagnostics (convergence, effective sample size, trace plots).

cr6_validity_of_outcome_measures.supporting_text: For the current study, we focused on cortical thickness measures of the 34 bilateral regions (averaged between left and right hemisphere) of the Desikian Killiany atlas parcellation (Desikan et al., 2006) as a part of the FreeSurfer (Fischl et al., 2004) output and the average cortical thickness across all 34 regions. | The data were processed using a standardized protocol (Craddock et al., 2013) of the FreeSurfer standard pipeline | As a first step, the measures were scanned for outliers. The criterion applied to mark a value as an outlier was if it was above or beyond 2 inter quartile ranges from the mean of all values for that region and hemisphere.

cr7_handling_of_confounding_variables.reason: Confounding variables are comprehensively addressed. Step 1: Basic confounders (age and sex) are explicitly modeled. Step 2: Multi-site effects are extensively addressed - this is the primary focus of the study. Step 3: Multiple harmonization approaches are described and compared. Step 4: The paper goes beyond normative modeling to evaluate confounding in clinical comparisons - testing whether site effects remain after correction and whether clinically meaningful variation is preserved. All four criteria are met (100%).
cr7_handling_of_confounding_variables.supporting_text: We propose a hierarchical Bayesian approach in which we include site as a random effect in the model, avoiding the exclusion of meaningful variance correlated with site by predicting site effects as part of the model instead of removing them from the data. | Using ANOVAs with site as predictor indicates that site cannot be predicted from the z-scores in the HBGPM control training set (p = 1) | In order to test whether our method is capable of retaining variance of interest, we applied the HBLM and HBGPM to the patient data set
